Loch Circuits: Riding Around Scotland's Great Lochs

Scotland's lochs are natural centrepieces for motorcycle day rides. A circuit around a major loch gives you a defined route with constantly changing perspectives — one shore sunlit, the other in shadow; one shore wild and roadless, the other dotted with villages. Here are the finest loch circuits for motorcyclists.

Loch Ness Circuit

  • Distance: 72 miles
  • Route: Inverness → A82 (northwest shore) → Fort Augustus → B862/B852 (southeast shore) → Inverness
  • Highlights: Urquhart Castle, Fort Augustus locks, the B862 — a far superior riding road to the busy A82. Falls of Foyers on the south shore.
  • Time: 2-3 hours riding, half a day with stops

Loch Lomond Circuit

  • Distance: 80 miles
  • Route: Balloch → A82 (west shore) → Tarbet → A83 → A815 → A814 (east shore) → Balloch
  • Highlights: The Bonnie Banks on the west shore, the narrowing of the loch at Tarbet, views to Ben Lomond. The east shore road through Drymen is quieter and more pleasant.

Loch Tay Circuit

  • Distance: 36 miles
  • Route: Killin → South shore road → Kenmore → A827 (north shore) → Killin
  • Highlights: Falls of Dochart at Killin, the crannog centre at Kenmore, Ben Lawers rising above the north shore. The south shore road is narrow and quiet — a hidden gem.

Loch Maree, Wester Ross

  • Distance: Not a full circuit (the south shore has no road), but the A832 along the north shore is 12 miles of stunning riding.
  • Highlights: Pine-covered islands, views to Slioch mountain, some of the oldest Scots Pine woodland in the country. Possibly the most beautiful loch in Scotland.

Loch Awe Circuit

  • Distance: 50 miles
  • Route: Dalmally → A85 (north shore) → B845 (south shore) → Dalmally
  • Highlights: Kilchurn Castle ruins, St Conan's Kirk (a stunning chapel on the lochside), the B845 through the forest on the quiet south side.

Loch Katrine, Trossachs

The road around Loch Katrine is limited (only the east end is accessible by public road), but the A821 Duke's Pass road between Aberfoyle and the Trossachs is one of Scotland's finest biking roads and gives wonderful loch views. Loch circuits are ideal day rides from a touring base. They're self-contained, varied, and give a sense of completion. Ride one shore in the morning when the sun lights one side, and the other in the afternoon when it lights the other.

Tips for Loch Riding

  • One shore is usually on a main road (busier, faster) and the other on a minor road (quieter, narrower). Ride the minor road for the better experience.
  • Lochs create their own microclimates — mist can linger over water when the hilltops are clear.
  • Shore-side parking spots and lay-bys are perfect for photos and coffee breaks.
  • Wildlife around lochs includes osprey, red squirrel, otter, and red deer. Keep your eyes open at the water's edge.
keyTakeaways: Loch circuits make ideal self-contained day rides from a touring base, with constantly changing perspectives.
On Loch Ness the quiet B862/B852 south shore beats the busy A82 for riding.
The Loch Tay south shore road and Loch Awe's B845 are quiet hidden gems away from the main roads.
Loch Maree in Wester Ross has no south-shore road but the A832 north shore is 12 stunning miles.
Ride one shore in the morning and the other in the afternoon to keep the sun lighting the water.

faq.q: Which shore should I ride on a loch circuit?
faq.a: Wherever possible, favour the minor road over the main one. On Loch Ness the B862/B852 south shore is narrower, twistier, and far quieter than the tourist-heavy A82. On Loch Tay the south shore road is a hidden gem, and on Loch Awe the B845 threads quietly through forest. The minor roads reward you with better views and a calmer, more engaging ride.

faq.q: How long does a loch circuit take?
faq.a: It varies with the loch. The compact 36-mile Loch Tay circuit is an easy half day with stops, while the 72-mile Loch Ness and 80-mile Loch Lomond loops fill most of a day once you factor in photo halts and coffee. Treat them as relaxed day rides from a base rather than a race, and build in time for the castle and waterfall stops.

faq.q: When is the light best around the lochs?
faq.a: Because one shore faces the other, timing matters. Ride the shore the morning sun lights first, then take the opposite shore in the afternoon when the sun has swung round. Lochs create their own microclimates, so mist can linger over the water while the hilltops are clear, which itself makes for atmospheric early photographs at lay-bys along the shore.

faq.q: What wildlife might I see on a loch ride?
faq.a: Loch shores are rich in wildlife. Keep an eye on the water's edge for otters and, in the right areas, osprey fishing, while red deer and red squirrels frequent the surrounding woodland. Lay-bys and shore-side parking spots make ideal quiet places to stop, watch, and photograph. Ride carefully near dawn and dusk when animals are most active near the road.
